title: Navigating the Storm: US–China Tariffs' Impact on Logistics
summary: Fuller maps the tariff shock from Chinese orders through ports, trucking, inventories and retail. Eisman probes denominators and challenges exaggerated claims that partial disruptions mean a complete stop. The interview distinguishes immediate freight-sector pain from later shortages, but its near-zero probability of a quick China agreement failed within twelve days. Conditional shortage and earnings scenarios require more care because policy changed. Fuller's extreme domestic-food share and net-food-exporter premises conflict with official data, while the proprietary freight statistics remain unverified.
assessment: Useful operational transmission analysis and explicit scope challenges coexist with a failed near-term political forecast and weakly verified freight extrapolations. Guest claims are kept separate from Eisman's scorecard.
speaker_map_notes: The normalized transcript names Steve Eisman and Craig Fuller inline throughout; dialogue confirms questions versus answers. Guest assertions are not treated as Eisman endorsements merely because he repeats them for clarification.
framework_points: Trace orders, production, bookings, arrival, warehouses and retail inventories separately.
Distinguish partial sector declines from complete economic cessation.
Separate import-accounting effects, survey sentiment and measured activity.
Keep the no-agreement counterfactual separate from an explicit probability forecast.
Check denominator consistency when moving from logistics jobs to trucking jobs.
tools_and_charts: FreightWaves high-frequency booking and truckload data, not reproduced in the episode.
China-US container bookings versus prior baseline and year earlier.
GDP import contribution and survey comparisons.
J.B. Hunt share-price drawdown and anonymous EPS estimates.
transcript_cautions: Recorded April 30, 2025 after the market close; published May 5.
The opening montage repeats the order-pause discussion; substantive timestamps are used.
Bookings, actual shipments, containers and baseline versus year-over-year changes are sometimes conflated.
The 450,000-500,000 jobs example moves from all logistics to trucking alone.
Food share has no calorie or tonnage denominator; the audit uses FDA supply and USDA spending evidence explicitly.
The J.B. Hunt call/tariff chronology is recalled uncertainly and is incorrect.

claims.speaker: Craig Fuller

claims.reason: The mechanism is plausible but the degree of circumvention and economic effectiveness are not established.
claims.next_check: Measure evasion rates, origin enforcement and export substitution.

claims.claim: Broad tariffs warn third countries that continuing to facilitate Chinese transshipment will provoke US punishment.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Inspect anti-transshipment provisions and enforcement actions.

claims.next_check: Inspect anti-transshipment provisions and enforcement actions.

claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Track concrete restrictions rather than grade the metaphor.

claims.next_check: Track concrete restrictions rather than grade the metaphor.

claims.claim: Cheap labor, weak constraints and US protection of sea lanes enabled China to become the manufacturing center.

claims.next_check: Use comparative manufacturing and shipping-security evidence.

claims.claim: US naval protection has largely removed the historic piracy threat around the Strait of Malacca.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Compare ReCAAP incidents and the contribution of regional versus US patrols.
claims.qualifications: The speaker corrects himself from eliminating to a less absolute formulation.
claims.reason: The speaker partially retreats from elimination; the relevant regional incident series was not fully inspectable in this audit.
claims.next_check: Compare ReCAAP incidents and the contribution of regional versus US patrols.

claims.claim: China-to-US container bookings have fallen about 65% from the pre-escalation baseline and roughly 35% year over year.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Obtain dated FreightWaves booking data, methodology and exact comparison dates.
claims.reason: A later port decline supports disruption but cannot verify this proprietary booking series or its shifting denominator.

evidence.title: May cargo results
evidence.finding: May loaded imports fell 9% from a year earlier and 19% from April; overall cargo fell 5%. This confirms a disruption, but does not verify a proprietary 65% China booking decline or a 35% decline in all-port monthly shipments.

claims.next_check: Obtain dated FreightWaves booking data, methodology and exact comparison dates.

claims.claim: Large US buyers often receive supplier credit, so halted deliveries leave Chinese manufacturers financing completed inventory.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Inspect supplier payment terms, receivables and inventory changes.
claims.reason: The cash-flow mechanism is coherent, but contract terms and prevalence across named buyers are unverified.
claims.next_check: Inspect supplier payment terms, receivables and inventory changes.

claims.claim: The tariff shock has stopped many deliveries without reducing China-US cargo flows to zero.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Distinguish bookings, departures, arrivals and total versus China-specific cargo.
claims.qualifications: This verdict applies only to continued trade, not the exact proprietary percentages.
claims.reason: Original China-origin container data show continuing May flow of 637,001 TEUs despite a 28.5% year-over-year decline.

evidence.title: May 2025 container import data
evidence.finding: The original trade-data provider reports May China-origin imports of 637,001 TEUs, down 28.5% year over year and 20.8% from April. Flow continued despite disruption. Monthly realized imports are not the same as earlier booking declines.

claims.next_check: Distinguish bookings, departures, arrivals and total versus China-specific cargo.

claims.claim: Booking and transit usually create roughly a three-week lag before China disruptions reach California ports.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Inspect actual booking-to-arrival distributions.

claims.next_check: Inspect actual booking-to-arrival distributions.

claims.next_check: Compare order books and production calendars by category.

claims.claim: Products with 30-40% gross margins cannot absorb a 145% tariff on their existing cost base without price or sourcing changes.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Verify customs value and retail-cost relationships for actual products.
claims.qualifications: Not a measured claim that all retailers have these margins; tariff base is customs value, not retail price.
claims.reason: Under the stated illustrative assumptions, the added duty exceeds gross profit.
claims.next_check: Verify customs value and retail-cost relationships for actual products.
claims.deductive_proof: For price P and imported cost C=(1-g)P, with g=.30 to .40, duty 1.45C=.87P to 1.015P exceeds original gross profit .30P to .40P. This requires customs value to equal the assumed imported cost and no offsetting adjustment.

proof.derivation: For price P and imported cost C=(1-g)P, with g=.30 to .40, duty 1.45C=.87P to 1.015P exceeds original gross profit .30P to .40P. This requires customs value to equal the assumed imported cost and no offsetting adjustment.

evidence.finding: The release initially estimated real GDP -0.3% annualized, real imports +41.3%, and private domestic final sales +3.0%. The import subtraction is accounting treatment alongside positive consumption and inventory components; the release was subsequently revised. 2024 nominal GDP was $29.1849 trillion.

claims.claim: Approximately 95-98% of food consumed in the United States is made domestically.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Specify supply, spending, calories or tonnage rather than interchange denominators.
claims.qualifications: The US can be predominantly self-supplying without the claimed extreme percentage being accurate; no calorie share was supplied.
claims.reason: FDA describes approximately 15% of overall food supply as imported; USDA estimates 15% of food-and-beverage purchases are direct imports. Neither supports 95-98% domestic supply.

evidence.title: Strategy for the Safety of Imported Food
evidence.finding: FDA describes approximately 15% of the overall US food supply as imported, far above the 2-5% implied in the interview. The document predates the episode.

evidence.title: Food import spending shares
evidence.finding: Direct imports were 15% of 2023 food and beverage purchases; 85% came through domestic production, which also included imported inputs. This spending denominator is not a calorie measure.

claims.next_check: Specify supply, spending, calories or tonnage rather than interchange denominators.

claims.claim: The United States is a net food exporter.
claims.speaker: Craig Fuller
claims.test: Use a defined value category and period; do not infer food security from a trade balance.
claims.qualifications: Verdict uses standard trade-value interpretation, not an unstated calorie or tonnage balance.
claims.reason: In 2024 the food, feed and beverage trade category had about a $50.8 billion deficit. USDA agriculture also had a deficit but is a separate denominator.

evidence.title: December and annual 2024 trade tables
evidence.finding: The 2024 food, feed and beverage category shows exports of $165.256 billion and imports of $216.058 billion. Goods trade with China was approximately $143.5 billion of exports and $438.9 billion of imports. These are value measures, not calories or tonnage.

evidence.title: May agricultural trade outlook
evidence.finding: Fiscal 2024 agricultural exports were $174.4 billion and imports $206.2 billion. Agriculture is a different category from food, so this deficit is supporting context rather than the food-supply denominator.

claims.next_check: Use a defined value category and period; do not infer food security from a trade balance.

evidence.finding: The memorandum excepted specified electronics headings, including 85171300, from reciprocal tariffs retroactive to April 5. Other tariff layers were not all removed.
